A 'fork' is just when a given miner chooses to run different code. What that happens, the blockchain 'forks,' and which ever version the majority of miners run becomes the dominant one. Since miners are heavily financially invested in the primary blockchain, real forks, where a significant percentage of miners change their code, almost never happen. There has been one large fork of the bitcoin blockchain, and that was because the bitcoin cash people insisted on running code to expand the block size while the majority of miners wanted to utilize the SegWit protocol.

As you can now see, bitcoin cash is not the primary blockchain, SegWit is the primary blockchain. Whenever the blockchain forks you get value on both block chains, I sold most of my Bitcoin Cash during the 'flippening' nonsense because I was aware that bitcoin cash didn't have majority miner support. I made a handy profit off people thinking the other way round.

Forks are an important part of the cryptocurrency economy, and every one who owns any of the forked block chain gets a vote in which one is the 'real' blockchain. Realistically though, it is in the self-interest of all miners to prevent anything tampering that would destabilize the block chain, and you can bet your ass that they read any and all code before implementing it. There is a network of thousands of people, acting in their own self interest, confirming the validity of any new code that could possibly be run to modify the block chain. That's why bitcoin has the most value; it has the most people running it, it has the most dependability, and it's value is not beholden to the behavior of even very large interested parties. Doesn't hurt that it has the most dispersion of value of all the cryptocurrencies either. No one owns bitcoin, something that can be said for few other blockchains.

Moving on to ereasure; Ereasure is only possible if the majority of miners all agree that a specific transaction did, or did not, occur. Practically speaking it's an impossible task in teh modern era of the cryptocurrency, but it was done once before bitcoin had any real value, and long before it was the most powerful computational network in human history. Some idiot tried a 51% attack against the few miners running the blockchain back then, and they decided to simply discount the transaction that the attack took place in. Nowadays it's not possible for major governments to stage such an attack as even the most powerful of government super computers pale in comparison to the distributed bitcoin network.

Let's describe this as an example: If you have 50 coins on Ledger "A", and it's forked, now there's Ledger "A" and Ledger "B", and you have 50 coins on Ledger A, and you have 50 coins on Ledger B. When a fork occurs to a blockchain it duplicates all the history of the forked block chain.

Any one who had 50 BTC (wealthy bastard that they are) before it was forked between BCH and the core BTC blockchain would have 50 BTC and 50 BCH. The forked ledger doesn't generate new coins, it generates a copy of the old ledger. They've doubled the amount of coins they have, but the two blockchains are in direct competition with each other. Eventually one will become dominant, and the way to make money is selling the non-dominant coins to purchase the dominant coins. It becomes a free-market exercise to see which new blockchain is valued more.

What a fork doesn't do is create new cryptocurrency at the current value. If you recall, when the BTC/BCH fork took place, BCH was valued significantly below BTC, and there was a lot of political fuckery that happened to try and prop it up as real competition to BTC.

If no wealth flowed into, or out of, the crypto during a fork, and if the general populace was perfectly evenly divided on which blockchain they preferred, then all a Fork would do is halve the value of the cryptocurrency and double it's supply. But because a fork requires running different code, the crypto-markets will universally have a preference for one or the other, so the value won't halve, it'll be an 80/20 split or something like that. Additionally, because wealth flows into the crypto markets faster than it flows out, you are likely to see the value of both blockchains remain as pretty significant, doubly so because most of the coins won't actually be utilized.

Splitting your cryptocurrency during a fork is a little bit of effort, and the market capitalization is determined by the total number of coins on a chain multiplied by the most recent averaged price at which one was sold. So if only 50% of people actually split their coins between ledger A and ledger B, then ledger B will only have 50% of the volume, but the market capitalization won't reflect that because it doesn't calculate the percentage of coins actively used (because it's impossible to do that). If that happens then what was an 80/20 split will look more like a 60/40 split in total capitalization, again, similar to what we saw when BTC and BCH split.

Tl;dr when a fork happens, the two combined cryptocurrencies hold the same amount of net wealth. Additionally, any one who owned coins on the original chain holds the same amount of wealth now divided between two separate chains. However, market movements, inaccurate market capitalization rates, and wealth flowing into the crypto markets create the illusion of inflation where there isn't any.

Forking is close to a company splitting shares (if you owned one at $100 now you own two at $50) where the new shares are under a different name. Then you get the same market shenanigans where people try and figure out which will be dominant and sell the ones that aren't.
